6.old: There is no legal definition of a penthouse in BC. On MLS, it's a style the listing agent picks for a unit, usually on the top floor of an apartment building. Some penthouses take up a whole floor. Others share the top floor with a few other units. Many have higher ceilings, a larger deck or a private roof deck, but none of that is guaranteed by the name.
6.new: BC has no legal definition of a penthouse. On MLS it is simply a style the listing agent chooses for a unit, normally on the highest floor of an apartment building. Some penthouses fill an entire floor, while others sit up top with a handful of neighbours. Higher ceilings, a bigger deck or a private roof deck are common, but the name does not promise any of them.

7.old: Because the tag is chosen by the agent, a few top-floor units never get it, and a few listings use "PH" in the unit number without the tag. When you're looking, I check the tag, the floor and the unit number together, so a good unit doesn't slip past you.
7.new: The tag is the agent's call, so some top-floor units never receive it, and some listings put PH in the unit number but skip the tag. I cross-check the tag against the floor and the unit number when I search for you, so a good unit doesn't slip by.

14.old: Every penthouse is a strata lot, so you're buying into a strata corporation under BC's Strata Property Act. A top-floor unit raises a few questions that lower floors don't.
14.new: Each penthouse is a strata lot, which means you join a strata corporation governed by BC's Strata Property Act. Living on the top floor brings up some questions that lower floors rarely raise.

16.old: A roof deck is often limited common property. That means it's common property set aside for one unit's use, not part of the unit itself. The strata plan and bylaws show who can use it, what you can put on it and who pays for upkeep. Ask whether hot tubs, planters or barbecues are allowed, since weight and the roof membrane matter.
16.new: A roof deck is frequently limited common property, meaning common property assigned to a single unit rather than being part of the unit itself. Check the strata plan and bylaws to learn who may use it, what can go on it and who covers upkeep. Find out if hot tubs, planters or barbecues are permitted, because weight and the roof membrane come into it.

20.old: Strata fees are usually based on unit entitlement, which is set out on the strata plan. A larger unit often has a higher entitlement and a higher monthly fee. The Form B Information Certificate shows the exact fee, any special levies and the bylaws in force.
20.new: Strata fees generally follow unit entitlement, which the strata plan sets out. A bigger unit tends to carry a higher entitlement and so a higher monthly fee. For the precise fee, any special levies and the bylaws currently in force, look at the Form B Information Certificate.

30.old: A penthouse is a top-floor unit that the listing agent has tagged with the Penthouse style. There is no legal definition, so confirm the floor and layout yourself.
30.new: In practice a penthouse is a unit on the top floor that its listing agent labelled with the Penthouse style. Since the term has no legal definition, verify the floor and layout on your own.

34.old: Not always. A roof deck is often limited common property, which is common property set aside for one unit. The strata plan and bylaws show who uses it and who pays for upkeep.
34.new: Not necessarily. Many roof decks are limited common property, meaning common property reserved for one unit. Check the strata plan and bylaws for who gets to use it and who pays to maintain it.

36.old: Strata fees are usually based on unit entitlement, which is set out on the strata plan. A larger unit often has a higher entitlement, so check the Form B for the exact monthly amount.
36.new: Fees usually come from unit entitlement, as listed on the strata plan. Bigger units often carry a higher entitlement, so the Form B will give you the exact monthly figure.

38.old: Read the Form B Information Certificate, the bylaws and rules, recent minutes, the depreciation report and the most recent financial statements. Look for roof, membrane and elevator items.
38.new: Start with the Form B Information Certificate. Then go through the bylaws and rules, the minutes from recent meetings, the depreciation report and the latest financial statements. Pay attention to any roof, membrane and elevator items.

40.old: No. White Rock is its own city with its own zoning and building bylaws. South Surrey is part of the City of Surrey, so permits and zoning come from Surrey.
40.new: No. White Rock runs its own zoning and building bylaws as a separate city. South Surrey sits within the City of Surrey, so Surrey handles its permits and zoning.

42.old: Unit numbers like PH1 help, but not every penthouse uses them and not every top-floor unit is tagged. I check the tag, the floor and the unit number together.
42.new: Numbers like PH1 are a good clue, but plenty of penthouses lack one and plenty of top-floor units are untagged, so I compare the unit number, the floor and the tag.
